IS4487 Week 10 - Assignment¶

Outline¶

Our Goals with this Project:

  1. Import and review the data
  2. Perform EDA and Clean Data
  3. Fit a model
  4. Test the accuracy of the model
  5. Use the model to predict on a new dataset (without the target)

Business Context AdviseInvest¶

You work on a small team of data analysts at AdviseInvest, a venture-backed startup. The Director of Sales at AdviseInvest has approached your team asking for help solving a staffing problem.

The Company¶

The company's mission is to provide tools and support to help ordinary people gain control of their personal finances. The company leverages technology to provide affordable financial advice to a national client base.

Customers who reach AdviseInvest's website go through five steps:

  • Open an account.
  • Complete a customer profile form with basic information about their background and finances.
  • Schedule a free phone conversation with a sales representative during a 1-hour window of time.
  • Attend the free phone conversation.
  • Buy a financial plan.
  • There are three types of financial plans: Beginner, Intermediate, and Advanced. Each is sold at a different price, and there are varying degrees of personalization. After a customer purchases a financial plan, the customer is assigned a financial planner who helps determine the customer's goals and advises the customer on spending decisions.

The Problem¶

Some customers are lost at each stage of the process. Steps 3 and 4 are particularly challenging because approximately 50% of those who schedule a phone conversation fail to pick up the call. This leads to inefficiencies from a staffing perspective.

AdviseInvest has 4 sales reps on staff during each particular 1-hour window. Each of the 4 reps is assigned 2 prospective customers per hour, which means that the company schedules a total of 8 phone calls per hour. The calls are outgoing: sales reps call customers who scheduled a phone conversation during that hour window.

Unfortunately, as noted above, many of the customers who scheduled a call do not answer. As a consequence, sales reps are often left underutilized. Moreover, they are underutilized unevenly. For example, it is possible that one sales rep will not do any sales calls during that hour, whereas another will be busy the entire hour with two calls. Sales reps have nothing to do when customers do not answer the scheduled phone call.

AdviseInvest Data Dictionary¶

Variable Description Type Code
customer_id Unique customer identifier Numeric
Answered Customer response Binary 0: customer did not answer scheduled call; 1: customer answered scheduled call
Income Customer income in US dollars Numeric
Female Customer gender Binary 0: male; 1: female
Age Age in years Numeric
Job Nature of job Categorical 0 : unemployed; 1 : entry level position; 2 : midlevel position; 3 : management/ self-employed/ highly qualified employee/ officer
Num_dependents Number of people for whom the customer provides maintenance Numeric
Rent Customer rents Binary 0: no; 1: yes
Own_res Customer owns residence Binary 0: no; 1: yes
New_car Recent new car purchase Binary New car purchase in the last 3 months: 0: no, 1: yes
Chk_acct Checking account status Categorical 0 : no checking account; 1: checking < 200 USD; 2 : 200 < checking < 2000 USD; 3: 2000 < checking < 35000 USD; 4: >= 3500 USD
Sav_acct Average balance in savings account Categorical 0 : no savings account; 1 : 100 <= savings < 500 USD; 2 : 500 <= savings < 2000 USD; 3 : 2000 < savings < 35000 USD; 4: >= 3500 USD
Num_accts Number of accounts owned by customer Numeric
Mobile Mobile phone Binary 0: customer provided non‐mobile phone for follow‐up call; 1: customer provided mobile phone for follow‐up call
Product Type of product purchased after conversation with sales rep Categorical 0: customer did not answer call; 1: customer answered but did not purchase a product; 2: customer answered and purchased Beginner plan; 3: customer answered and purchased Intermediate plan; 4: customer answered and purchased Advanced plan

Reflection:¶

1.1. What stands out in the initial preview? Any columns or rows that seem unusual?

✍️ Your Response: 🔧¶

1.1. A handful of values can't be real. Two customers have negative incomes (-$65,600 and -$15,430), one is 132 years old, and one has 3,345 accounts. Another has 8 when everyone else has 0 to 4. female loaded as text because one row says "M" instead of 0 or 1, new_car is blank on 2 rows, and 3 rows are exact duplicates.

The bigger surprise is how repetitive the file is. There are 29,504 rows, but ignore customer_id and only 469 of them are different. 453 customer profiles show up exactly 64 times each, just under different IDs. That means the test set will be full of rows the model already saw in training, so its accuracy will probably look better than it would on customers it has never seen.

product stands out too. It's 0 for every customer who didn't answer and 1 to 4 for every customer who did, so it's really the target under another name, and nobody knows it until after the call.

Step 2: Data Preparation¶

2.1: Data Cleanup¶

Do the following:¶

  • 2.1 Check for and remove any outliers
  • 2.2 Consider fixing any missing data (should you delete the record or impute the value?)
  • 2.3 remove any variables, like customer_id, that are not helpful in predicting the target variable (hint: are there any variables that are available only AFTER the customer has answered, and wouldn't be useful in predicting?)
  • 2.4 Clean up the data and put it in a new dataframe named "df_clean"
In [4]:
# Exact duplicates from step 1
df_clean = df.drop_duplicates()

# 2.1 Outliers: values that can't be real
df_clean = df_clean[
    (df_clean['income'] > 0) & (df_clean['age'] <= 100) & (df_clean['num_accts'] <= 4)
].copy()

# 2.2 Missing and bad data. 'M' is male, which the dictionary codes as 0.
df_clean['female'] = df_clean['female'].replace('M', '0')
df_clean = df_clean.dropna(subset=['new_car'])

# 2.3 customer_id is only a label, and product isn't known until after the call
df_clean = df_clean.drop(columns=['customer_id', 'product'])

# 2.4 Check the result
print('Rows before cleaning:', len(df))
print('Rows after cleaning: ', len(df_clean))

Reflection:¶

2.5 Explain the steps that you took to clean outliers and missing data. Why did you chose the approach that you used?

2.6 Which variables did you remove, and why?

✍️ Your Response: 🔧¶

2.5 The outliers weren't just big numbers, they were errors: two negative incomes, an age of 132 and 3,345 accounts. I counted 8 accounts as one too, since every other customer has 0 to 4. I deleted those 5 rows because there's no way to know what the real values were. I didn't use an IQR cutoff. Income is skewed right, so it would have thrown out real high earners, and chart 3.2 shows they're some of the least likely customers to answer.

For missing data, new_car was blank on 2 rows. I deleted them instead of imputing, since a guessed yes/no is just noise and 2 rows out of 29,504 won't be missed. The "M" in female I could actually fix, because the dictionary codes male as 0. Dropping the 3 exact duplicates as well took the data from 29,504 rows to 29,494.

2.6 customer_id, because it's just a label and has nothing to do with whether someone picks up. And product, because it's filled in after the call. A 0 means the customer didn't answer, so leaving it in would hand the model the answer, and it wouldn't exist yet for a customer we're deciding whether to call.

Reflection:¶

3.6. Which variables show the strongest relationship with the target variable?

3.7. Did you find any variables that have a weak relationship with the target variable? Should they be removed?

✍️ Your Response: 🔧¶

3.6. Checking account balance, by a wide margin. 79% of customers with over $2,000 in checking answered against 39% of customers with no checking account, and it has the strongest correlation with answered at 0.35. Income is next (-0.22) and runs the other way. The customers who didn't answer earn more, and nobody earning over $111,000 answered at all. Savings balance (0.18), number of accounts (0.12) and having a mobile phone come after that, with 74% of mobile customers answering against 53% of everyone else. Age matters more than its 0.07 correlation suggests because it isn't a straight line. 19 to 24 year olds answered 42% of the time and 35 to 39 year olds 70%.

3.7. num_dependents is the weakest at -0.01, basically nothing, so I removed it. job (-0.06) is weak too, but I kept it, since a tree only splits on a variable when it helps and ignores it otherwise.

female also has a small correlation (-0.07), but mostly because only about 5% of customers are women. The gap itself is big, 40% of women answered against 56% of men. I removed it anyway. This model decides who gets a sales call, and gender shouldn't be the reason a customer doesn't get one.

4.4: Calculate the accuracy¶

This should be better than the base probability, or you have failed in your objective

Do the following:¶

  • Calculate the probability for your tree

y_pred = tree_model.predict(X_test)
tree_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred)

print(f'Tree accuracy:    {tree_accuracy:.2%}')
print(f'Base probability: {base_rate:.2%}')
print(f'Difference:       {(tree_accuracy - base_rate) * 100:.1f} percentage points')

Tree accuracy:    74.42%
Base probability: 54.67%
Difference:       19.8 percentage points

Reflection:¶

  1. What is the difference between the probability from the model compared to the base probability?
  2. Is this difference a significant amount for the business?

✍️ Your Response: 🔧¶

  1. The tree is right 74.4% of the time. The base probability is 54.7%, which is how often you'd be right just assuming everyone answers, so the tree is 19.8 percentage points better. Put another way, about 1 in 4 predictions is wrong instead of close to 1 in 2.

  2. Yes, it's a real improvement in knowing which calls will connect. Accuracy doesn't say what the mistakes cost, though. Skipping someone who would have answered gives up $75 in profit, while a wasted call only costs $25, so the model has to be judged on profit too, which is what step 5 does.

Step 5: Evaluate the Model¶

Assumptions

One of the simplifying assumptions we will make in this project is that all the customers who answer the phone will purchase a product. (This assumption is actually verified by the data.) To model "answered" in this case is therefore equivalent to modeling "purchased."

There are costs and benefits in this case. We will assume that customers purchase a product for 100 dollars. This was the average cost of AdviseInvest products, according to the Director of Sales. Also, as we learned in the interview, the agent time to make the sale is worth 25 dollars. Profit would therefore be $75 dollars for an answered call and a purchase. In sum:

Benefit: True positive. The customer is predicted to answer, does answer, and purchases a product for 100 dollars for a profit of 100 - 25 = 75.

Cost: False positive. The customer is predicted to answer, but does not answer, so there is a loss of 25. (We assume the agent cannot schedule another call at the last minute, or spends the entire time slot trying to make the call.)

When you create a calculation you can use:

  • True answered * 75 -> These people purchased
  • False answered * 25 -> You can't schedule another call

For this exercise, we propose that customers who are not predicted to answer will not be called, so there would be no benefits and no costs for them.

Do the following:¶

Calculate the Profit Using the Model

In [18]:
tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()

model_calls = tp + fp
model_profit = tp * 75 - fp * 25

print(f'Called and answered:    {tp:>5,} x $75 = ${tp * 75:,}')
print(f'Called, no answer:      {fp:>5,} x $25 = -${fp * 25:,}')
print(f'Profit using the model: ${model_profit:,}')
print(f'Profit per call:        ${model_profit / model_calls:.2f} ({model_calls:,} calls)')

Called and answered:    2,141 x $75 = $160,575
Called, no answer:        426 x $25 = -$10,650
Profit using the model: $149,925
Profit per call:        $58.40 (2,567 calls)

5.2 Compare to the Default Profit¶

Do the following:¶

  • Calculate the profit (revenue - costs) that would be expected if all customers are called

Notes:

  • We can consider this a baseline case for profit since it does not require a model
  • In other words, to calculate profit in this baseline scenario treat the customers who answer as true positives treat the customers who do not answer as false positives.
In [19]:
answered_total = y_test.sum()
no_answer_total = len(y_test) - answered_total
default_profit = answered_total * 75 - no_answer_total * 25

print(f'Called and answered:     {answered_total:>5,} x $75 = ${answered_total * 75:,}')
print(f'Called, no answer:       {no_answer_total:>5,} x $25 = -${no_answer_total * 25:,}')
print(f'Profit calling everyone: ${default_profit:,}')
print(f'Profit per call:         ${default_profit / len(y_test):.2f} ({len(y_test):,} calls)')

gap = model_profit - default_profit
print(f"\n{'The model' if gap > 0 else 'Calling everyone'} earns ${abs(gap):,} more")

Called and answered:     3,224 x $75 = $241,800
Called, no answer:       2,675 x $25 = -$66,875
Profit calling everyone: $174,925
Profit per call:         $29.65 (5,899 calls)

Calling everyone earns $25,000 more

  1. What is the difference in profit between calling all customers and calling customers that are recommended by the model?
  2. Is this a significant amount for the business?

✍️ Your Response: 🔧¶

  1. Calling everyone makes $174,925 on the test customers and the model makes $149,925, so the model earns $25,000 less. It skips 2,249 customers who wouldn't have answered, which saves $56,225 in wasted calls, but it also skips 1,083 who would have, and that's $81,225 in profit we never make. A missed sale costs three times what a wasted call does, so the trade loses money.

  2. Yes, but it depends how you count it. The $25,000 treats a skipped call as worth nothing, but AdviseInvest books a fixed 8 calls an hour, so a slot the model frees up can go to another customer. Per call the model almost doubles profit, $58.40 against $29.65, because 2,141 of its 2,567 calls get answered. When the reps' hours are the limit, that per-call number is the one that counts.

5.3 Tune the Model¶

Do the Following¶

  • Create a new version of the tree with new parameters
  • Calculate a new probability

Notes:

  • Adjust the size or shape of the tree, then test the accuracy
  • Keep changing these parameters until you end up with a tree with accuracy that is better than the initial model
In [20]:
for depth in [4, 5, 6, 8, 10, None]:
    candidate = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', max_depth=depth, random_state=42)
    candidate.fit(X_train, y_train)
    accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, candidate.predict(X_test))
    print(f'max_depth={str(depth):<5} leaves={candidate.get_n_leaves():<4} accuracy={accuracy:.2%}')

# With no depth limit the tree scores 100%, which isn't believable. It's the copies from
# step 1: every test row has an identical row in the training set, so a deep enough tree
# just memorizes the answers. Most of what the deeper trees gain comes from that, so I
# only went one level past the first tree.
tree_tuned = DecisionTreeClassifier(criterion='entropy', max_depth=5, random_state=42)
tree_tuned.fit(X_train, y_train)

y_pred_tuned = tree_tuned.predict(X_test)
tuned_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_tuned)
cm_tuned = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_tuned)
tuned_profit = cm_tuned[1, 1] * 75 - cm_tuned[0, 1] * 25

print(f'\nTuned tree accuracy: {tuned_accuracy:.2%} (first tree {tree_accuracy:.2%})')
print(f'Tuned tree profit:   ${tuned_profit:,} (first tree ${model_profit:,})')

Step 6: Conclusion¶

Reflection:¶

6.1: Did we improve our profit using the model?

6.2: How could the model be utilized by the business?

✍️ Your Response: 🔧¶

6.1 Not in total dollars. On the test customers, calling everyone makes $174,925, the first tree $149,925 and the tuned tree $157,525. Tuning closed some of the gap, but both trees still skip too many people who would have answered. Per call is a different story. The first tree makes $58.40 a call against $29.65 for calling everyone, and with only 8 call slots an hour, that's the profit that matters for AdviseInvest's staffing problem.

All of these profit figures run high, too. The $75 assumes everyone who answers buys a plan, but 2,432 customers in this data answered and bought nothing (product = 1).

6.2 I'd use it less to decide who gets called and more to decide how the calls get assigned. Score each customer when they book, then give every rep a similar mix of likely and unlikely answerers, so nobody sits through two no-shows while someone else has two live calls. That's the uneven workload the Director of Sales described, and the tuned tree expects 449 of the 1,000 new customers to answer, so there's something to plan around.

Two changes before using it. The tree says "answered" once the chance passes 50%, but with $75 to gain and $25 to lose, a call pays for itself above 25%, so when reps have open slots the cutoff should come down. And it should be checked against real call results for a few weeks first, because the copies in this data make its test accuracy look better than it really is.
